author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Harassment won’t stop a son’s search for his missing father
content:
Marklen Lariosa, son of missing Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) labor organizer William Lariosa, speaks during a rally in Davao City on the first anniversary of his father’s disappearance on April 10, 2025. Photo by Kath Cortez/Davao Today

“Family members searching for their disappeared loved ones have to endure threats and harassment from state forces on top of the terrible uncertainty and emotional turmoil they are already going through.”

Is it a mistake for a son to demand justice and accountability?

Marklen, son of disappeared labor organizer William Lariosa, raised this question following the recent incident of harassment and surveillance he experienced. Members of his family were alarmed after two unidentified individuals were looking for his residence on the night of October 25.

He told Bulatlat that this was the first time such an event had happened since his father, a labor organizer under Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) Southern Mindanao, was abducted in Quezon, Bukidnon, on April 10, 2024.

Marklen could not think of other possible reasons, suspecting that the incident may have something to do with his continuing involvement in campaigns and mobilizations that demand the surfacing of Lariosa. “Is it a mistake for a son to search for his missing father?” he further asked.

Read: After 2 years, son laments continuing disappearance of Mindanao labor organizer

Neighbors of the Lariosa family in their hometown in Davao de Oro province were the ones who encountered the two individuals. They reportedly wore helmets and were on board a black motorcycle, introducing themselves as “collectors” when they were asked.

For Marklen, the response and presence of the two raised suspicions. Aside from the fact that they visited the community around 7 p.m., which is outside the regular working hours, Marklen said that he did not apply for any financial loan.

After the incident, he was concerned for the safety of his family, prompting them to lodge a blotter report with the barangay. However, he stood firm that it won’t stop him from continuing his cause.

Desaparecidos, an organization of families and friends of enforced disappearance victims, denounced the incident, urging the government to put an end to this kind of harassment.

“Family members searching for their disappeared loved ones have to endure threats and harassment from state forces on top of the terrible uncertainty and emotional turmoil they are already going through,” JL Burgos, Desaparecidos chairperson, said in a statement.

Rights groups Karapatan and the Center for Trade Union and Human Rights (CTUHR) also expressed strong condemnations about what happened.

Marklen, a member of the National Board of Desaparecidos, has raised a possibility that the two individuals who recently visited their neighborhood might be connected to those who visited their house several times prior to the disappearance of his father.

He said they were visited by individuals who allegedly introduced themselves as state agents once in 2022 and three times in 2023, accusing Lariosa of being involved in communist insurgency. There were warnings, he added, that they would get dragged into it if they would not cooperate.

The series of visits was reportedly the primary reason why Lariosa was forced to take refuge in Bukidnon. Marklen affirmed that his father, who remains missing, had been a labor organizer.

On July 8, the Supreme Court required certain commanders and elements of Philippine Army units to comment on the petition for review on certiorari filed by the family.

Read: Military ordered to reply to missing Mindanao labor organizer’s case

Since 2024, KMU Southern Mindanao has documented 57 cases of human rights violations against its members and organizers.

The labor group released a statement on October 24, presenting the faces of some individuals, including former high-ranking New People’s Army (NPA) member Roberto Rosete Jr., who allegedly harassed KMU’s leaders and members.

Read: Groups decry surveillance of KMU office in Southern Mindanao

Marklen called for an end to any form of harassment and intimidation against families of the disappeared, pointing out that achieving justice is their only goal. (RVO)

title: Cops arrest 3 University of Makati students after anti-Pax Silica protest
content:
Police headlocking a UMak studen. (Photo from Anakbayan-UMaK)

Three students of the University of Makati (UMak) who participated in a protest against Pax Silica were arrested earlier today, November 13, in Bonifacio Global City, Taguig City.

According to Panday Sining UMak, uniformed police officers and intelligence personnel in plainclothes surrounded the demonstrators, confronting them over an alleged unauthorized assembly and confiscating their placards.

In a statement, Anakbayan UMak condemned the violent, arbitrary arrest. “This is how the rotten government of Marcos Jr. treats students who are peacefully expressing their sentiments,” the group said.

Video footage from Karapatan National Capital Region showed that a police officer punched a female student who attempted to free another arrested student. A police officer was captured headlocking one of the arrested students. who can be seen to be put in a headlock by a police officer in another video report.

Karapatan NCR also reported that a paralegal who responded to the forceful arrest was threatened with charges by police officers.

title: IMF, WB cause misery for marginalized communities
content:
The Counterdocket exposed the harms caused by the IMF-WB.







BANGKOK – For 80 years, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank (WB) brought suffering to many communities in the Global South.




On October 15, their stories were heard at the Counterdocket in Bangkok, Thailand where the two Breton Woods institutions also held their annual meeting from October 12 to 18.  




Dubbed as Our Voices Count! A Counterdocket, it brought together movements to challenge extractive systems and demand greater accountability from the IMF-WB. The Counterdocket exposed the harms caused by the IMF-WB. From the Support to Parcelization of Lands for Individual Titling (SPLIT) project of the WB Group in the Philippines to Lithium mining in Argentina, these testimonies became public records of the IMF-WB’s effects on communities.

author: Shannia Cabuello
title: Artists, Ayta sing vs Pax Silica
content:
Photo by Shannia Angel Cabuello

Artists and other advocates amplified their opposition against a US-led initiative through song.

On November 6, an artist group launched the anti-Pax Silica anthem “Get Off Our Lands” in a solidarity night filled with protest songs.

Produced by the Concerned Artists of the Philippines (CAP), the song was accompanied by a documentary music video featuring the Ayta community in Sitio Kalangitan, whose ancestral lands and natural resources are threatened by displacement and plunder.

Through the song, CAP aimed to expose the false promises behind the Pax Silica and to condemn those in power who allowed it.

Cultural performances and solidarity messages completed the program as part of the Trump Out campaign and the ‘12 Days of Protests’, building up the major protest actions on November 16 and 17.

Ayta elders also attended the solidarity night and expressed their strong rejection of Pax Silica, chanting “Ako Labay Ya Pax Silica!” (I don’t like Pax Silica!).

They led a community dance ritual to drive away “bad spirits,” which they associate with the Pax Silica Initiative and the impending visit of US President Donald Trump for the ASEAN Summit.

Ayta Chieftain Nelson De Guzman countered the statement of Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) President Joshua Bingcang that no Indigenous community would be affected by the Pax Silica Initiative. He said that no proper consultation was conducted within their community.

“They learned that they were being driven away from their land even before they knew about the project,” said Sandiwa Network project coordinator Gina Cambronero.

“The Pax Silica will kill our future. We nurtured our lands. We cannot allow foreigners to claim it,” said Ayta Indigenous woman Tessie Sanchez.

Sanchez told Bulatlat that planting rice, taro, and sweet potato helped support her seven children. She feared that the signing of the agreement could dry their water sources and take away their farmlands.

“The ruling class used the term pax which meant peace. But is there peace in it? They use it as instruments for deception,” Cambronero said.

“We just want peace in our tribe and in our land,” De Guzman said in the song’s documentary music video.

Around 20,000 peasants and 15,000 Ayta could be reportedly displaced once its Artificial Intelligence hub was established on the 1,620 hectares of land in Tarlac.

The anthem started by introducing the Philippines as a friendly Southeast Asian country that shares its homeland to everyone, even to foreign ones.

The music video explained that Ferdinand Marcos Jr. volunteered to give the agricultural and ancestral lands in Tarlac to the United States to establish an Economic Security Zone.

CAP said that the establishment of an Artificial Intelligence hub in Tarlac and the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) in Subic Bay, Clark, Manila and Batangas that claims of job creation and economic security are false promises. The group said that it only “prioritizes corporate profits and militarization, fueling war for the US benefit.”

“In the past years, we have always been at a disadvantage with US relations. There are already several trade agreements that only lead to our losses,” said Attorney Rey Cortez of National Union of People’s Lawyers (NUPL).

Cortez added in a solidarity message that it only allowed for the United States to mine the country’s lands and determine how to exploit its resources. He described the government’s marketing of the country’s environment and sovereignty as unconstitutional, as only the Filipinos are allowed to explore the Philippines’ critical minerals.

“Development should not be measured by the number of investments, infrastructure, and technology advancements. Its effect on the people, community, and environment must also be analysed,” said College of Social Work and Community Development Dean and CAP member Justin Nicolas.

Arthur Cadungon of CAP and writer of Get Off Our Lands said that the anthem is not just for the fight against the Pax Silica Initiative, but also a song of protest against the reclamation of Manila Bay, Laguna Lake, and Pasig River Expressway (PAREX).

“An example of this is the Laguna Lake, which before sources at least 40% of protein food sources like mussels and freshwater fish tilapia,” said Environmental Advocates group Nilad coordinator Samantha Yzabel.

She added that fishing has become difficult for the communities near Laguna Lake as the destruction of ecosystems and pollution worsens. She also stressed that the Manila Bay and Pasig River are being destroyed, while communities continue to be displaced and deprived of livelihood.

Cadungon dedicated the song to the trees that were cut along the Quirino highway, and for the Filipinos who were drowned by flood and were neglected by the people in power.

“This is also a fight with the courageous people of the Kasibu community in Nueva Vizcaya, around the nation, and other countries that are being stripped bare by imperialists,” Cadungon said.

Artists and cultural workers strengthened their rejection of the Pax Silica that facilitates the use of Artificial Intelligence saying that it undermines human creativity.

“Trump’s visit means taking away my workforce. It means building of AI hubs that would replace years of artist’s struggle in honing their crafts,” handcrafter Aila Bathan said.

Just like the Ayta Indigenous Peoples and communities in Central Luzon, Bathan said that Pax Silica means death of their lives and livelihoods.

“True prosperity promotes people’s dignity, strengthens communities, nurtures the environment, and advocates for overall well-being,” said Dean Nicolas, calling on the Filipinos to be critical and stand firm for social justice.

CAP Secretary-General Edge Ungayuren emphasized that once farmers that cultivate the lands are threatened, even ordinary Filipinos are affected. “We believe that we must take a stand in this issue because it would kill our lands, bodies of water, farmers, and Indigenous Peoples. Our culture is rooted in our lands and bodies of water. If these will be gone, our culture will also be gone,”

CAP urged artists, cultural workers, and the public to use their art and the anti-Pax Silica anthem to take their resistance on the streets and get imperialists off the nation’s land. (AMU, DAA)

content:

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: ‘Get Off Our Lands’ political pop vs  Pax SIlica
content:
Photo by Shannia Cabuello/Bulatlat

It was a hot night on November 6 and Z compound, a food park at Teachers’ Village, was already brimming with enthusiasts for the world premiere of the anti-Pax Silica song anthem “Get Off Our Lands” by the Concerned Artists of the Philippines (CAP).

Highlight of the night was the launch of the music video, enhanced by a separate lyric video, and the actual performance of CAP’s music pool.

The song starts in a slow tempo, then pulled off unsuspectingly into a high-energy sound by the rhythm of various instruments and the piercing wails of Bayang Barrios. Soaring vocals join in, combined with addictive hooks and riffs that sustain the track’s hype and momentum. The melody is sharp and catchy, flowing seamlessly into a songwriting that has easy recall yet nails it as a serious political critique.

Without a doubt, the song title sets the core message, but the punch is delivered by the chants “Tutulan, labanan, reject Pax Silica!” which can draw even a crowd into a sea of resounding voices and clenched fists.

“Get Off Our Lands” is indeed a battlecry, a sonic weapon, against the US-led Pax Silica. An initiative or agreement in collusion with the Marcos Jr regime, Pax Silica would plunder the country’s critical minerals for the US war machine. Its plan to set up Artificial Intelligence hubs would also deprive communities of scarce water resources and energy and poison the environment. Even artists are up in arms as they might lose not just their jobs but the authenticity of their art and craft as well.

In the video, the cries of the Aytas of Capas, Tarlac, probably the first victims of displacement, has sounded off the people’s indignation. It is an emotional, yet serene plea to stop, reject, or shot down Pax Silica, not just for themselves but also for all those who will be affected. That CAP made the Aytas, this peace-loving indigenous community, speak for themselves is a stark contrast to the destruction and violence that awaits them, and the nation in due time.

It is a grim scenario. But the night did not leave the viewers and listeners in quiet rage. Then CAP’s music pool commanded the stage. The explosion of energetic sound with astounding raw vocals brought bodies suddenly jumping on their feet, eager to sway and vibe, and without a prompt turned to the lyric video, singing, chanting, dancing. The crowd, mostly millennials and GenZs seemed to have lost it. To everyone’s applause one band member even quipped – “this is not AI”.

Political pop is not just about poverty and sufferings, domination and violence. As much as it is expository, it is also celebratory. That one night in November proved it. The awakening was palpable, though many of those who attended were probably already woke. The crowd knew the fears, the dangers, the darkness of Pax Silica. Still the spirits were high. Optimism seemed to fill the air seeing the people’s defiance on screen: whether in the Aytas’ soft words, the sincerity of the artists, the militance of mass leaders, the fiery protest actions layered on top of the music’s vibrancy. Much as Pax Silica brings doom, the people’s collective struggle depicted in the song or video brings hope and much more. And the crowd felt it and the response was electric.

In addition, the passion, the conviction, and the emotion that artists have poured into “Get Off Our Lands” was borne out of their own experiences. So it has become and remains organic. The artistas ng bayan spent days with the Aytas in their own community, immersed in their own life stories, felt their surroundings, and delved into their culture.

And so it was that the making of the song did not become a private treasure. The Aytas participated and contributed some lines. So did a roster of composers, songwriters, performers, recording engineers and fellow bands who supported, gave comments, reactions, put in a word or two, before the song ‘s debut. From a shared experience with the Aytas the song became a truly collective collaboration of artists who believed in the same goal.

Now all it takes is to spread and amplify the song in a manner so massive it awakens people to the dangers of Pax Silica and move them into action. CAP has summoned a clarion call to all interested parties to do covers, play the song in all types of events or performances, and saturate social media.

November is also the month that US President Donald Trump is coming to the 49th ASEAN Summit in the Philippines, and anticipation is high that the Pax Silica agreement will be signed. By then the No to Pax Silica movement shall be ready, Trump will feel the heat of being unwelcomed, and slammed by the music “Get Off Our Lands”.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Investigate police, doctors involved in Duterte’s ‘drug war’
content:
Forensic pathologist Dr. Raquel Fortun, also a member of the commission, presents one of the questionable certificates during the commission's truth-telling session last Friday. (Truth Commission photo)

The Truth Commission has called on the Philippine government to investigate the police officers’ misconduct and promotion and the doctors’ questionable death certificates in the course of the “drug war” campaign of former President Rodrigo Duterte.

“My son was alive when they arrested him, but they killed him. They could’ve let him live. They did not show mercy, they planted drugs and guns,” Marissa Lazaro, mother of extrajudicial killing victim Cristopher Lazaro, said in Tagalog during the commission’s truth-telling session.

The Truth Commission pointed to a failed system for investigating deaths, marked by careless police and forensic work, and little concern for victims’ families. Lazaro’s account also showed that the police officers were asking money from her, indicating a potential trail of corruption.

Cristopher, 20, and Alberto Paragas, 32, died in police operations on August 5, 2017 in Marilao, Bulacan. Police reported that the two resisted (nanlaban) after an alleged attempted holdup. Cristopher’s friends also died hours earlier in Bocaue, a separate town in Bulacan.

Lazaro added, “They asked me to sign a waiver, indicating that I consented to their illegal operation. I did not sign it. They told me: the day will come that I will seek their help. I told them, what help could you give my son? You killed him. He’s already dead.”

A similar incident happened to Marissa Quiamco, sister of Alberto, after she paid the P10,000 fee to release the cadaver of her brother. A police officer asked her and Alberto’s partner to sign a document, indicating consent for the operation but they refused to sign.

“I wish I could fight for my brother. Even my neighbors asked me to file a complaint. But I told them: we don’t have money. We don’t have the capacity or resources to get a lawyer,” Quiamco said during the truth-telling session. “I’m only earning enough to help my mother and father.”

In October, an analysis of public records by the Truth Commission recorded a pattern that commanding police officers were promoted and reassigned, instead of being subjected to criminal and administrative sanctions.

Lito Patay, who commanded Batasan police station that killed 108 people in drug operations during his term, was named chief of the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) in Central Luzon.

In Caloocan, the commission’s own records documented 284 killings in 2016, before the leadership of Chito Bersaluno in the City Police. During his watch, 105 more deaths were recorded from February to August 2017. He was removed from his post after the killing of Kian delos Santos. However, he was made police director of Bulacan Province in 2018 and promoted to the rank of brigadier general in 2022.

In 2020, human rights organizations flagged the reassignment of Debold Sinas, former chief of the Central Visayas Police Regional Office, to the National Capital Region. The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) Regional Office said back then that Sinas’ watch in Central Visayas was marred by unresolved killings linked to the illegal drugs trade and the anti-insurgency campaign “Oplan Sauron.” Duterte appointed him as the Philippine National Police Chief on November 9, 2020, serving a six-month term. A year after, he was appointed as an undersecretary of the Office of the President.

Read: [LIST] Gross human rights violations under Debold Sinas

“Any inquiry must look at promotions as closely as it looks at cash payments,” said Christopher Magno, the commission’s executive director and an expert on state violence in the Philippines. “No police officer should gain in any way from the blood of people killed outside the law.”

Former Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO) General Manager Royina Garma, who also served as Cebu City police chief under the Duterte administration, revealed the incentivization of police officers through the “Davao Model” in a quad committee hearing of the House of Representatives in 2024.

“First is the reward if the suspect is killed. Second is the funding of planned operations. Third is the refund of operational expenses,” Garma said, stressing that the rewards started from P20,000 ($343.95) to P1 million ($17,197.50), depending on the profile of the suspects. She said that the rewards were only meant for killings, not for the arrest of the drug suspects.

During the quad committee hearing, it was also revealed that rewards for anti-drug operations by the police involved several key figures, including then-Special Assistant to the President Bong Go, an individual known as “Muking” from the Presidential Management Staff, a “Pedro” from the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group, and former National Police Commission (Napolcom) Commissioner Edilberto Leonardo, who handled the distribution of the payments.

Read: Duterte’s testimony affirmed that drug-related extrajudicial killings a state policy — right groups

Questionable death certification

The Truth Commission also called on the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) to investigate the medical doctors behind the questionable death certificates of extrajudicial killing victims.

A letter submitted by the Truth Commission on November 9 reads: “Accurate death certification is essential to establishing the truth about the circumstances of a person’s death. Where death certificates contain inaccurate, incomplete, or potentially misleading information, families may be deprived of an accurate official record of what happened to their loved ones.”

In the 150 extrajudicial killing victims examined by forensic pathologist Raquel Fortun, who is also a commissioner of the Truth Commission, at least 13 death certificates listed causes of death that did not match her findings. Among these were the cases of Alberto and Cristopher.

Fortun’s findings on Alberto’s forensic examination indicated that the manner of death was homicide. His death certificate stated no clear reason and labeled “for autopsy.” Fortun’s team tried to ask for an autopsy report but to no avail.

Christopher’s death certificate and medico-legal report issued by the Philippine National Police also did not match. The former document indicates that the cause of death was a “gunshot wound (to the trunk) and left lower extremity”, while the medico-legal stated “gunshot wound (of the) head and left lower extremity.”

She also questioned whether the doctor who documented ligature marks on Christopher’s wrists had been free to challenge the police. “This is very glaring. The pictures of the crime scene were also very limited and messy. The documentation of the scene is so wrong.”

The letter requested the PRC, through the Board of Medicine, not only to investigate the doctors and the death certification process, but also to determine professional accountability, help protect and preserve the evidence of “drug war”, and examine whether similar practices occurred in other cases.

They also asked the PRC to work with the Philippine Statistics Authority, local civil registrars, and relevant health authorities in correcting the death certificates. The Philippine Medical Association (PMA)’s Ethics Committee will also be helpful in examining possible violations of the professional ethics.

“We emphasize that the purpose of this request is not to prejudge the responsibility of any physician, but to ensure that questionable death certifications are properly investigated, that relevant evidence is protected, and that accountability is pursued where warranted and in accordance with due process,” the letter added.

“They already killed our loved ones, now, they’re vilifying them. I will persevere in speaking up to let the public know the true circumstances of my son’s death. Not all victims of the war on drugs are drug addicts. And even if they’re addicts, it is not a justified reason to kill them,” Lazaro said. (RTS, DAA)

author: Arnold Padilla
title: What’s at stake in Trump’s Manila visit?
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s upcoming visit to Manila for the ASEAN Summit happens in the wake of intensifying struggle between the U.S. and China for economic, technological, political, and military dominance in Asia. Washington aims to consolidate its strategic position in Southeast Asia, with the Philippines under Ferdinand Marcos Jr. playing an increasingly important role in advancing U.S. imperialist interests.

Trump arrives politically battered. The sweeping Republican defeat in the November 3 midterm elections, which handed both houses of Congress to the Democrats, represents a powerful repudiation of his administration’s policies. Trump’s unpopular U.S. war against Iran and his aggressive tariff policies and their disastrous economic consequences, such as rising living costs, contributed to widespread dissatisfaction among American voters.

The defeat further exposes the political crisis confronting U.S. imperialism. It reflects growing domestic opposition to policies that impose enormous economic and social costs on the American people while sustaining Washington’s aggressive military interventions and global ambitions.

But Trump’s weakened domestic position does not mean that the White House will abandon its imperialist agenda abroad. On the contrary, the administration may seek to demonstrate U.S. power through new military, economic, and diplomatic agreements. Trump could use his visit to Manila to project strength and secure strategic commitments to counter the political setback at home.

The central objective of Washington’s ASEAN agenda is to preserve U.S. supremacy in the face of China’s expanding economic and military power. Southeast Asia occupies a crucial place in this rivalry. It sits astride strategic maritime routes and contains vital manufacturing centers, mineral resources, emerging digital markets, and production networks essential to the world economy.

For U.S. imperialism, maintaining influence over ASEAN means safeguarding its military reach while securing access to markets, technology infrastructure, critical minerals, and industrial supply chains. The U.S. seeks to organize these strategic assets around its own economic and national-security priorities, particularly by reducing dependence on Chinese-controlled production networks.

At the same time, China is expanding its own economic and strategic influence through trade, investment, infrastructure, and military power. This competition between rival great powers seeks to expand their influence over the region’s resources, markets, territory, and political decisions.

Washington’s military agenda was made explicit during the ASEAN defense ministers’ meetings in Cebu in October, when Pete Hegseth, Trump’s so-called Secretary of War, proposed a new framework for U.S.–ASEAN defense cooperation.

Under the language of maritime security and interoperability, Washington seeks to deepen military coordination, intelligence sharing, joint exercises, and naval cooperation with Southeast Asian governments. The proposal complements the expanding network of U.S. military alliances and access arrangements across the Indo-Pacific. It aims to strengthen its First Island Chain strategy to encircle and contain China. On the sidelines of the Cebu meeting, U.S. and Japanese defense officials discussed implementing a more effective denial-defense posture along this chain.

With its geographical location, the Philippines has become a crucial platform for this strategy. Under Marcos Jr., U.S. military access under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) has expanded from five to nine designated Philippine facilities. Washington and Manila are also increasing joint military exercises and deployments of advanced missile and unmanned systems. These arrangements strengthen the capacity of U.S. forces to operate in the South China Sea and potentially respond to a Taiwan Strait conflict.

So far, only two ASEAN countries have formal defense treaties with the U.S., namely the Philippines and Thailand. But all the other members, except for Myanmar, have various forms of extensive defense or military cooperation arrangements with the U.S. However, unlike its Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) and related pacts with the Philippines, not all agreements with other ASEAN countries grant U.S. troops access to military installations, allow combat deployments, or entail an obligation to support U.S. military operations.

Hegseth’s proposal aims to move beyond separate military arrangements with individual ASEAN countries toward a more coordinated, ASEAN-wide structure for defense cooperation. Such a framework could strengthen the U.S. military’s regional presence and operational coordination without necessarily creating a formal military alliance. It will build on existing regional initiatives such as the ASEAN-U.S. Maritime Exercise (AUMX), the Southeast Asia Cooperation and Training (SEACAT), and other military exercises between ASEAN and the U.S. and American allies in the Indo-Pacific like Japan, Australia, and South Korea, focusing on naval coordination, maritime security and surveillance, and military interoperability.

Unlike the U.S., China lacks formal military treaties with any ASEAN member. However, it maintains defense cooperation memoranda of understanding with all of them except Myanmar, with which it nevertheless sustains substantial military equipment supplies, training, and defense ties. It also participates in the ASEAN-China Maritime Exercise (ACMX) as a regional initiative and maintains several bilateral and multilateral exercises with ASEAN members.

In terms of forward bases and military presence, the U.S. has several naval and air facilities in Thailand (U-Tapao airfield and Sattahip Naval Base) and Singapore (Changi Naval Base, Sembawang facilities and Paya Lebar Air Base), in addition to the nine EDCA sites in the Philippines, that allow the deployment of troops, prepositioning of supplies, and logistical support. China counters this with military infrastructure recently built in mainland Southeast Asia, specifically the Ream Naval Base in Cambodia and the Ban Keun aviation facility in Laos. Aside from the EDCA sites, the U.S. is also reinforcing its presence in the Philippines by deploying advanced weapons systems in strategic areas facing Taiwan and the South China Sea, while building defense-industrial infrastructure to support its military logistics and mobility through the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC). In response, China has fortified its position in the disputed maritime features of the South China Sea, establishing a military presence in the Spratly Islands with long airstrips, hangars, naval support facilities, and reportedly even air-defense and anti-ship missile systems.

The increasing militarization of Southeast Asia amid intensifying U.S.-China competition is exposing the people of the region to massive death and destruction. Such danger is aggravated by the political crisis the Trump regime faces following the midterm elections. It could further escalate regional tensions as Trump becomes more desperate and aggressive in projecting U.S. power abroad and asserting its control over territories it deems part of its spheres of influence to consolidate domestic support. To be sure, U.S. long-term strategic objectives in the Indo-Pacific have continued across successive Republican and Democratic regimes, but Trump’s post-midterm political calculations could further accelerate the region’s militarization and escalate tensions.

Battleground for strategic industries and supply chains

Another achievement Trump would likely seek during his Manila visit is finalizing an agreement with the Philippines to build an advanced manufacturing park within the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC). The 1,620-hectare Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park is a vital project for the Trump regime, as its success bolsters the feasibility of its Pax Silica initiative to counter China’s control over chokepoints of artificial intelligence (A.I.) supply chains, which have become a key arena of inter-imperialist competition for economic and military supremacy. Pax Silica is part of the broader U.S. strategic agenda to contain China and its rapid expansion.

Launched in December 2025, Pax Silica seeks to establish secure supply chains involving critical minerals, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, energy infrastructure, and A.I. technologies among the U.S. and its trusted allies. It aims to strengthen American influence over the technologies and industrial inputs increasingly regarded as essential to economic and military power. Southeast Asia plays an important role in this strategy because of its substantial mineral resources, established electronics manufacturing industries, growing digital markets, and its location along crucial international trade routes.

A major challenge for the U.S. is how to break China’s grip on the region’s critical mineral resources, the most important raw materials to build A.I. and its infrastructure. China has overwhelming dominance in Southeast Asia’s mining investments, mineral processing, exports, and purchases. Indonesia, for instance, holds the world’s largest nickel reserves, accounting for 44% of the total, and China accounts for around 75% of Indonesia’s nickel refining capacity. The Philippines ranks sixth, and almost 72% of its nickel ore and concentrate exports go to China, while 28% go to Indonesia, with the former likely processed by Chinese refineries. Dismantling such monopoly control makes Pax Silica’s success in the Philippines high on Trump’s agenda for his visit to Manila.

China, meanwhile, is pursuing its own strategy to consolidate and expand its influence over the international A.I. supply chains and digital economy. A significant development was the establishment of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) in July 2026, which presents itself as an inclusive intergovernmental institution that promotes cooperation, AI capacity building, and more equitable international governance.

Aside from the Philippines, Singapore is the only other ASEAN member among the 26 Pax Silica signatories. On the other hand, WAICO includes seven ASEAN countries among its 38 members: Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Myanmar, Malaysia, and Vietnam.

The ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), scheduled to be signed at the Manila Summit, provides a potentially far-reaching framework through which the U.S.-China competition over A.I. supply chains could unfold.

Although negotiated by ASEAN member states, DEFA is being developed in an environment dominated by American and Chinese technology corporations. Its provisions on digital trade, cross-border data flows, electronic commerce, digital payments, and A.I. cooperation could profoundly influence who controls the region’s emerging digital economy. For the U.S., expanded ASEAN digital integration offers opportunities to consolidate its dominance in cloud computing, digital platforms, A.I. systems, financial technologies, and data infrastructure.

Resist imperialist domination and war in Southeast Asia

Trump’s upcoming Manila visit underscores how Southeast Asia is increasingly becoming a major theater for the competing economic, geopolitical, and military ambitions of the U.S. and China. Whether through military alliances and forward deployments, control over critical minerals and advanced technologies, or the reorganization of regional production networks, the two rival powers are seeking to secure their respective spheres of influence at the expense of the region’s sovereignty and the interests of its peoples.

For the Philippines, the stakes are particularly high. The Marcos regime is allowing Washington to use the country as a frontline military platform against China while facilitating greater U.S. control over strategic infrastructure, industries, and resources. Under the guise of strengthening national security and attracting investments, these arrangements threaten to deepen the country’s economic dependence, undermine its sovereignty, and expose the Filipino people to the catastrophic consequences of a possible regional war.

Trump’s visit must therefore be met with determined opposition to U.S. imperialist intervention, militarization, and economic domination. The Filipino people must join hands with the peoples of Southeast Asia to resist foreign domination, oppose preparations for war, and assert their right to determine their own political and economic future.

The peoples of Southeast Asia have nothing to gain from being drawn into an escalating confrontation between rival powers. What the region needs is not deeper subordination to competing imperialist agendas, but genuine cooperation based on mutual benefit and respect for national sovereignty and the democratic rights and aspirations of its peoples. (DAA)

title: Peryodiko
content:
Photo from the Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas

Maganda ang teknolohiya kung mapapakinabangan ng karamihan.

May nagbabasa pa kaya ng peryodiko? Alam pa kaya ng kabataan ang mga katulad na salitang pahayagan at diyaryo?

Baka mas pundamental pa ang tanong: May nagbabasa pa kaya? Totoo bang wala nang masyadong kultura ng pagbuklat ng anumang nakaimprenta dahil mas gusto ng mga taong manood na lang ng bidyo?

Kung sabagay, higit pa sa peryodismo ang isyu. Analog o digital? Nobela o pelikula? Lumang midya o bagong midya? Pero saglit lang. Kailangan ba talagang mamili sa dalawa? Hindi ba puwedeng pagsabayin ang luma’t bago?

Kung gagamit ng ilang salita sa wikang Ingles, hindi ito usapin ng “conversion” kundi “convergence.” Posibleng gamitin ng lumang midya ang bagong teknolohiya para mapalakas ang mga katangian nito. At sa konteksto ng peryodismo, nagdesisyon ang maraming peryodikong gumawa ng mga website at account sa iba’t ibang social media platform.

Para sa mga peryodista, kailangang pumunta kung nasaan ang masa. Ito ang dahilan ng literal na pagbisita sa mga komunidad, lalo na sa mga liblib na lugar na tila napag-iwanan ng kabihasnan. Ito rin ang magpapaliwanag kung bakit pinapatulan pati ang TikTok sa paghuhubog ng opinyong pampubliko. Naglalaan din sila ng oras para makipagtalastasan sa social media kahit na hindi pinapansin ang mga personal na atake.

Dahil sa mabilis na pag-unlad ng teknolohiya, totoo namang lumang-luma na ang mga tinaguriang sinauna. Pero kapansin-pansin ang ebolusyon ng print para isama sa diseminasyon ng impormasyon ang teknolohiyang digital.

Gayundin ang kaso ng mga programa sa radyo dahil mayroon na silang kaakibat na teleradyo para marinig at makita ang balita, pati na ang nangyayari sa loob ng booth habang nagbobrodkast. At para naman sa mga programa sa telebisyon, uso na rin ang simultaneous live streaming.

Ngunit para sa mga lugar na mahina o walang internet signal, patuloy na namamayagpag ang lumang midya. Mas nakadepende sila sa radyo o telebisyon para sa pinakahuling balita. Nakakatulong din naman ang peryodiko para sa dagdag na pagsusuri kahit na hindi agad-agad na nakukuha ang kopya. Kaya hindi naman masyadong nahuhuli sa balita ang mga nasa liblib na lugar basta’t may mga matiyagang magsusubaybay at maghahanap ng paraan.

Maganda ang teknolohiya kung mapapakinabangan ng karamihan. Pero kung ang kalidad at bilis ng internet ay depende sa panggastos, parating mapipilitan ang mahihirap na pagtiyagaan ang mabagal na koneksiyon.

Para sa karamihang naka-prepaid na account lang sa kanilang mobile phone, mas gagamitin ang mga libreng opsiyon para ma-access ang social media accounts pero malamang na hindi maki-click ang link papunta sa buong teksto ng balitang nasa website ng mga organisasyong pang-midya. Kaya ang mangyayari, headline lang o maikling bahagi lang ng balita ang posibleng mabasa.

Anong klaseng opinyon ang mabubuo kung limitado lang ang impormasyon? Hindi ba’t mas mainam na gawing libre ang internet para sa lahat? Bakit kailangan pa kasing pagkakitaan ang teknolohiyang dapat na maging tulay para sa epektibong diseminasyon ng impormasyon?

Pero labas ng internet access, kailangan ding pangalagaan ang mga tinaguriang luma. Patuloy na kilalanin ang ambag ng print, radyo at telebisyon, lalo na ang kanilang paggamit ng teknolohiya sa gitna ng nagbabagong panahon. Hindi hiwalay ang pag-aaral ng bago sa pagkilala ng luma. Katulad ito sa pag-intindi ng kasalukuyan batay sa aral ng kasaysayan.

Uso pa ba ang peryodiko? Tandaang may mga nagbabasa pa naman. Hindi naman mawawala ang print media sa kabila ng pag-unlad ng teknolohiya. Mahalaga pa rin ang tuloy-tuloy na paglilimbag lalo na’t kinakailangan ang malalim na pagsasakonteksto.

title: Rural communities face continuing violence amid militarization
content:
Photo by Viggo Sarmago/Bulatlat

Under the blazing sun in front Camp Aguinaldo, palay hats stood out together with the line of banners. It was not a celebration for peasants — but a plea to end militarization, violence, and to serve justice for Negros 19 killed in Toboso, Negros Occidental on April 19, 2026.

Farmers and fisherfolk play a vital role in sustaining the nation’s food security and economy, yet they are the ones who struggle the most to survive.

Pamalakaya’s National Vice Chairperson Ronnel Arambulo stated in his speech during the fourth day of peasant month protest on October 19, that the administration does not aim to protect the life and rights of the people, farmers, and fisherfolk, but to protect the ruling class, the foreigners, and the people in power for their own personal interest.

Fisherfolks are also facing harassment that disrupts their lives. According to Arambulo, there are recent reports of intimidation in Binangonan, Rizal, where fisherfolk were called by Maritime Police to appear at the municipal hall. They were later summoned to renounce and abandon Pamalakaya.

This kind of intimidation is not confined to the province of Rizal, as similar deployments have also been reported in other regions.

Nida Barcenas from Karapatan-Bicol stated that the 9th Infantry “Spear” Division of Philippine Army or at least ten battalions of men in uniform were scattered around six provinces in Bicol region.

During the “Stakeholder and Media Fellowship Night: Episode 1 – Kaakibat sa Kapayapaan,” event of 9th Infantry Division held on April 18, 2026 at Camp Elias Angeles, Maj. Gen. Aldwine I. Almase recognized the efforts of national agencies, local government units, media personalities, and other stakeholders in countering alleged local terrorist activities to ensure peace and safety in the Bicol region.

For Karapatan-Bicol , however, these achievements actually meant human rights abuses against farmers communities. As of March 2026, Karapatan has recorded 46 political prisoners in Bicol — 9 of them are women, with 22 arrested under Marcos Jr. administration. In his four year term in the government, two enforced disappearances and 38 extrajudicial killings have also been documented.

Red-tagging, violence, and land grabbing continue to disrupt the lives of Bicolanos, Barcenas said.

“To this day, residents of Masbate continue to appeal for help amid alleged land grabbing by Governor Kho. Farmers are being driven off their lands, and those who resist are killed and red-tagged as NPAs, [New People’s Army]” Barcenas said.

The issue involving Governor Antonio Kho is also part of the problem regarding land dispute over the Pecson Estate in Cawayan, Masbate. Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) stated that Kho took over a portion of 1,807-hectare estate, forcing more than 100 farmers off the lands they have cultivated for years.

The agrarian conflict has also been associated with reports of killing involving peasants in Cawayan. A human rights report from Karapatan revealed cases including killings of farmers named Pancho Versaga and Renard Remulta on October 28, 2022 in Sitio Villaluna, Barangay Itom-Bato, Cawayan. These two were among more than 100 farmers tilling a 450-hectare portion of the Pecson Estate within land seized by Kho in Masbate.

Karapatan has declared Masbate as Bicol’s killing fields due to an increasing number of victims who had been killed under Marcos Jr. regime’s counter-insurgency war on the province.

One of the heinous cases was the killing of a farmer couple Aimee and Jover Villegas, a two-hectare land caretaker. The military said that the couple died under armed encounters. However, their injuries contradict this claim as Aimee’s throat, chin, and neck had been slashed, while Jover sustained gunshot wounds in the nape and back.

Echoing this concern, Grace Nabian from Amihan-Negros called for a stop to the militarization in rural communities.

She questioned killings, abduction, and threats against farmers, stressing that land reform, and access to quality education for their children are what they need.

She also pressed his demand to hold Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) accountable for various deaths in their land including Negros 19.

During an afternoon mass in a collective protest campout in front of the Department of Agrarian Reform, Sol Santuyo, mother of Maureen Santuyo, emphasized the long-overdue demand of farmers that were ignored by the government.

“From then until now, our farmers have had one cry, but those in power deliberately turn a deaf ear. I hope a better way is found, so that no more youth would have to risk their lives just to help our farmers,” Santuyo, whose daughter was among those killed in Toboso, said.

Various organizations along with other student activists continue to call for justice for Santuyo, Alyssa Alano, RJ Ledesma, and Errol Wendell, Lyle Prijoles, Kai Sorem, and others but to all farmers, fisherfolk, journalists, and residents who were killed, abducted, threatened, and deprived of land and rights. author: Shannia Cabuello
title: Molbog community exposes agenda behind land-use projects
content:
They turned our ancestor’s burial sites into dumping grounds.

“They want to take everything so we insisted on coming here to express ourselves. We will embrace our land even if they harass us. We will not give it even if we get hurt.”

Molbog community member Anjilon Flores from Balabac Palawan stressed this point as Molbog indigenous peoples travelled to Metro Manila ahead of US President Donald Trump’s visit.

They aim to amplify their resistance against the Department of Environmental and Natural Resources’ Enhanced National Greening Program (E-NGP) and the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA).

Along with multi-sectoral groups and environmental advocates, they exposed the E-NGP and EDCA as tools of imperialist war and resource plunder, threatening the life, livelihood, culture, and ancestral lands of the Molbog people.

Long before Spanish colonial rule, the Molbog community have been the traditional stewards of Balabac island, depending on coconut farming, shifting cultivation, fishing, and harvesting seaweeds for livelihood.

“Palawan is a key biodiversity area and known to be the last ecological frontier of the Philippines,” Bianca Intia of Kalikasan Timog Katagalugan (TK) said at a press conference on October 26.

It shelters several endemic animal and plant species, including Philippine Mouse-deer which are exclusively found in Balabac and nearby islands.

Flores described their fields as prosperous with cassava, banana, corn, peanuts, and rice, making it their community’s main source of income for decades.

For them, lands are sacred that require ancestral permission before undertaking any activities like when entering the land, performing rituals, planting, harvesting, and cutting trees.

Born in Balabac, Flores cannot accept the prohibitions imposed by the E-NGP in using their resources. “They would restrict us from cutting trees which we use for firewood. This is also the livelihood for most of us. What will happen if they forbid us? Our livelihood will also be gone.”

Bangsa Molbog leader Emmanuel San Esteban lamented the encroachment of Balabac Air Base on their homes, sacred prayer grounds, and burial sites in Barangay Catagupan without any consultation with their tribal officials.

“They turned our ancestor’s burial sites into dumping grounds. The mountains where we do our rituals were flattened,” San Esteban said.

The local authorities said that the remains of their ancestors would be transferred to a different location. However, this is against the principles and culture of the Molbog tribe.

The indigenous residents dread the impact of both projects, as it begins to disrupt their peace, routines, and tradition.

They stressed that access to their land has been restricted, limiting the products they could gather from the forest.

According to DENR, the E-NGP was signed to rehabilitate the estimated 1.2 million hectares of the remaining unproductive, denuded, and degraded forestlands by 2022. It also aimed to maintain and protect existing forests.

This was already implemented by the DENR in several areas in Balabac where trees were planted in Barangay Catagupan, Agutayan, and Indalawan.

The communities worried about fines for damaging plants under E-NGP while clearing farmland. Cutting a tree must also be replaced with a hundred more trees and a Php 6,000 ($94) fine.

Kalikasan TK underscored that E-NGP did not aim to benefit communities but only to carbon offset the Ipilan Nickel Corporation’s deforestation and mining operations in Brooke’s Point, Palawan.

The Molbog people also expressed concerns that monocropping and fast-growing plant species under the E-NGP could affect forest biodiversity and native vegetation.

“The E-NGP is within our ancestral domain, for which we had applied for a Certificate on Ancestral Domain Title (CADT),” said San Esteban, questioning how the project progressed faster than their CADT application.

They first filed their CADT application in 2004 but the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) only certified the application in 2019. To expedite the process, the NCIP required them to pay at least Php 1.6 million ($25,092.33). Their CADT remains pending.

San Esteban said that Balabac Air Base in Barangay Catagupan also pushed through because of the NCIP’s manipulation of the Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) process.

“Our mayor has been conducting surveys in our area. Only eight people agreed to the project while the majority of more than 100 said no,” San Esteban said. The NCIP conducted similar surveys in other areas and used the results to support documents for the project’s approval.

Earlier this year, the Southern Tagalog Exposure (STeX), along with environmental defenders, visited Balabac to investigate the project’s impacts. It would be built along Molbog’s 26,000 hectares of ancestral domain and waters, specifically in Barangay Catagupan with a population of 2,000 people.

Marky Casaquite of STeX said that residents believe that a headquarters building would be ready in around two months. Some of those who are living on the land were hired for the EDCA site construction with a promise of a stable job. They later learned that they would only be employed for this specific facility.

Since its construction, residents have also reported incidents of physical assault and violence inflicted by municipal and military officers.

“I am the one being targeted by the soldiers wearing facial coverings. They do not introduce themselves when they threaten me,” San Esteban said.

When he raised their concerns about road restrictions to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), San Esteban experienced being kicked in the back by municipal officers. He tried issuing a blotter but the police declined to document the incident.

“So you know, if something happened to me, they are the ones to blame. They said straight to my face that they will soften my head and dump it somewhere,” he said.

San Esteban also criticized the unannounced live military exercises that sowed fear among their children. Foreign military soldiers were also being deployed in their area.

“The children are being scared. They were covering their ears because they did not inform our community that they would fire their guns,” he said in an interview.

According to the Balabac Air Station’s Base Development Plan, the EDCA site would cover approximately 301 hectares of land for 45 facilities that include firing range, solar farm, solar power plant, and Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) Hangar.

The Hangar would serve as aircraft staging and maintenance, logistical sortie and distribution hub, and civil military coordination center.

Earlier this year, the US army brought a rocket launcher to Balabac Island to conduct a temporary live fire simulation. Molbog people were aware of the ongoing conflict between the US and China, but contested that it is not enough basis to use ancestral lands for war.

“I hope those foreigners will be expelled from our lands. Since they got here, all they brought are restrictions and deception,” San Esteban said.

“The destruction of Balabac, Palawan is multifaceted in cause and consequence. The construction of the EDCA air base and the implementation of the E-NGP prioritize US strategic and corporate interest over the welfare of the Molbog community and the environment,” Intia said in a statement.

National Coordinator of Bai Indigenous Women’s Network Kim Falyao stressed that these are also experienced by the locals in Dupax Del Norte and Kasibu due to large-scale minings, the Igorot due to renewable energy projects, the Tumandok due to Jalaur Mega Dam, and the Ayta due to the Pax Silica Initiative.

“Marcos Jr. markets our lands as sources of minerals and wealth that serves the greed of the United States, building Philippine and US bases, camps, and facilities where they store weapons and conduct military exercises,” said Falyao, condemning the militarization that only threatens, bombs, and protects these projects.

Mong Palatino of Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (BAYAN) said that these aggressive developments in critical ecosystems are global preparations for imperialist war and plunder.

“Stop land grabbing, investigate those who inflict violence, and put them in jail. We hope the soldiers will be removed from our area so they can no longer disturb us,” San Esteban said.

On the approaching visit of US President Donald Trump, Falyao said that Indigenous Peoples would reiterate their calls to drive away the greedy US imperialist that plunders, destroys the environment, and kills the Indigenous Peoples lives and livelihood.

“Hope is not lost. The Filipino people are not afraid to express their indignation. Witness this on Trump’s visit to the Philippines during the ASEAN Summit,” Palatino said. (RTS, DAA)

title: Women on the frontlines defending land, life, and livelihood
content:
Across the Philippines, one of the world’s most disaster-prone countries, women are at the forefront of struggles to defend their communities against displacement, environmental destruction, and development aggression. From the mountains of Luzon to the coastal communities of the Visayas and Mindanao, they are fighting to protect the land and resources that make life possible.

In Kasibu, Nueva Vizcaya, about 300 women are actively involved in a long-running struggle against large-scale mining. They help maintain six community barricades that have blocked mining operations since 2007. Among the companies seeking to operate in the area is North Luzon Mineral Resources Corporation (NLMRC), whose government-issued exploration permit covers 4,456 hectares of land, threatening farms and watersheds that sustain thousands of residents. On November 8, 2013, the storm surge in Tacloban began at 7:00 a.m. and lasted until 8:30 am, submerging the city in seven meters of water. “Atop their roof, we witnessed the cries of people who could not be rescued as they were swept by the floods,” Laag said. The typhoon left thousands of people dead, millions displaced, and destroyed 90 percent of the city. Twenty-three people of those killed were from Paraiso.

title: The women of Davao Oriental protecting Balete Bay
content:
Amid the warming climate and the looming impacts of large-scale extractive mining projects, women like Peralez, Millomeda, and Decena, from fishing, farming, and religious backgrounds across Mati City have come together to protect one of the most ecologically critical areas in their town. 







By Michelle Mikiko Pagaran




Along the coast of Balete Bay, women farmers, fisherfolk, advocates, and church workers across Mati, Davao Oriental are coming together and turning to collective action and organic farming to protect their coasts, and adapt to extreme weather impacts of climate change.







A small mangrove grows amid thick aerial root networks in Balete Bay, Davao Oriental

. 

(Photo by Michelle Pagaran)







Tucked quietly along the coast of Mati, Davao Oriental is Balete Bay, a small inlet along the southern border of the province. Known as a breeding ground for various fish species, reef species and lobsters, the bay is of great ecological significance. A marine inlet, its cove-like structure hosts seagrass beds, diverse reef fisheries, and abundant mangroves.




A sanctuary of corals, mangroves, and commercially vital fisheries, the bay is important for local fisherfolk who depend on it for their livelihood. It serves as a breeding ground for shellfish and wild lobster fry.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Grieving without graves
content:
Families of enforced disappearance victims gather in a mass, offering tribute to their loved ones. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.

The commemoration of All Souls Day may be different for the loved ones of enforced disappearance victims (desaparecidos) but their annual gathering is a symbol of determination in their continuous search.

“We gather here together because we don’t have a grave to mourn at,” said Edith Burgos, vice chairperson of Karapatan and president of International Coalition Against Enforced Disappearances (ICAED).

Burgos is the mother of Jonas Burgos, a farmer-activist who was forcibly disappeared on April 28, 2007 at Ever Gotesco Mall, Quezon City. For almost two decades, she has been active in campaigning to surface Jonas and other desaparecidos.

“It might not be now, but I am sure that we will see justice. That even just a few of our loved ones will finally surface. There is zero success (rate) in searching for the disappeared here in the Philippines. Our hope remains,” Burgos said.

Some of the families have been searching for more than four decades, since the dictatorship of Ferdinand Marcos Sr., father of the current president Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

“My parents and my siblings died without seeing the body of my brother (Levi), without justice,” said Xcy Ybañez, brother of Cebu-based activist Rolando “Levi” Ybañez who was forcibly disappeared on July 11, 1985. On that same day, Redemptorist priest Fr. Rosaleo “Rudy” Romano was also forcibly disappeared by military agents.

Spanning administrations from Marcos Sr. to Marcos Jr., Karapatan and Desaparecidos documented at least 1,900 victims who had never surfaced as of this writing. While there is a law that criminalizes enforced disappearance, there has been no successful prosecution.

“Grieving is the processing of the loss of our loved ones,” said Ligaya Portajada, wife of labor activist Armando Portajada Sr. who was forcibly disappeared on July 14, 1988. “But for us in Desaparecidos, our grief and sorrow are never-ending, not until the surfacing of our loved ones. I wish for this crime to stop. Our loved ones are not criminals, they are only helping the marginalized people.”

Portajada Sr. was the Coca-Cola workers’ union president when he was abducted. Human rights defenders like him are often the target of enforced disappearance, affecting not only their families but also the communities they serve.

“Dad loves his family and friends. But most of all, he loves the people of Cordillera,” said Gabrielle Chuwaley Capuyan, daughter of indigenous rights activist Dexter Capuyan who was forcibly disappeared together with Gene Roz Jamil “Bazoo” De Jesus on April 28, 2023. “He chose to offer his strength to serve the indigenous peoples and farmers of Cordillera.”

Capuyan recalled that the communities they visited to find her father’s whereabouts is the reason to hold on to hope: Dexter was described as youthful, always ready to help, finding comfort in watching sitcoms, laughing amusely, with a dimple and posture resembling a certain actor from the series Boys Over Flowers. “It never fails to make us smile.”

Dexter and Bazoo were among the recent victims under the current administration. A year after, two other activists disappeared, namely veteran labor organizer James Jazmines and environmental activist Felix Salaveria Jr.

Their families filed petitions for writ of amparo and habeas data. On August 12, 2025, the Court of Appeals (CA) declared Dexter and Bazoo as victims of enforced disappearance, contrary to the outcome of the police investigation. Similarly, writs of amparo were also issued to Jazmines and Salaveria last year

Desaparecidos Philippines wrote to the Supreme Court (SC) to review the writs of amparo and habeas data for its “persistent ineffectiveness” for nearly two decades, without a single success story.

Read: Not one surfaced despite court orders, families demand review of legal remedies

“The government agencies, who were supposed to find our father, had shown us their apathy and incompetence. It is as if not a single life is at stake,” said Salaveria’s eldest daughter Felicia Ferrer. “Is there value to the decision of the Courts, if until now, my father has not yet surfaced? When justice remains elusive for all our fathers, mothers, children, and loved ones?”

Since the court orders did not result in the surfacing of their loved ones, Burgos earlier flagged that the process is long when it’s supposed to be a “swift” remedy. She said that state forces are uncooperative and hostile to the families and that there is no thorough investigation despite orders from the court. She added that no one is cited in contempt for not following.

More than 100 families, friends, and advocates gathered during the mass, followed by a short symbolic program to honor the desaparecidos as white roses were tied to the portraits of the victims and their names were recited.

“They frequently told us to move on and accept it as it is,” said Desaparecidos chairperson JL Burgos, filmmaker and brother of Jonas. “But how can we accept it if our questions remain unanswered, our loved ones remain missing, and without justice?”

While enforced disappearance is defined as a state-perpetrated or state-sanctioned crime, JL said that perpetrators are shielded by an impenetrable shroud of impunity. It is this impunity, he said, that is behind the fact that enforced disappearances continue to this day.

He called on the Philippine government to enforce the Anti-Enforced Disappearance Law. He also urged for the ratification of the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance, the only core international human rights treaty that the Philippines has not yet ratified.

“With the government dead set on denying us the truth, the November 2 gathering is ultimately an act of defiance,” JL said. “We declare that we have not forgotten our missing loved ones, we have not stopped searching for the truth behind their disappearance and calling for them to be surfaced, and we will not yield to the state’s attempts to threaten, harass or intimidate us.” (RTS, DAA)

author: Maverick Avila
title: ‘Long fight ahead after ethanol spill in Tañon Strait’ – lawyer in landmark case
content:
Wastewater from an ethanol spill discolors Bais Bay, the Philippines’ Negros Oriental province, on Oct. 28, 2025, days after ethanol wastewater spilled into the bay, causing significant damage to coastal and marine ecosystems. Image courtesy of MarGale Bancairen.

Despite the somewhat funny concept, they were serious about their goal: Stop the oil exploration in the Tañon Strait by Japan Petroleum Exploration (JAPEX).

In 2007, Philippine environmental lawyer Rose Liza Eisma-Osorio and four other law professors in Cebu City sat around laughing at an idea: representing marine mammals in court.

Despite the somewhat funny concept, they were serious about their goal: Stop the oil exploration in the Tañon Strait by Japan Petroleum Exploration (JAPEX). The protected seascape between the islands of Cebu and Negros is home to 14 whale and dolphin species, as well as coral reefs and mangrove forests. The Japanese energy company performed seismic surveys and drilled an exploration well, which drove away dolphins and whales from the strait.

It was an ambitious plan, as animals had never been named as petitioners. Eisma-Osorio and fellow lawyer Golly Estenzo Ramos filed the first petition representing the resident marine mammals in December 2007. Their colleagues filed a second petition on behalf of fishing communities directly affected by the exploration activities.

The case, Resident Marine Mammals of the Protected Seascape Tañon Strait v. Secretary Angelo Reyes, went on for several years. In April 2015, the Philippine Supreme Court ruled to void the contract that allowed the exploration, development, and exploitation of petroleum resources within the Tañon Strait.

Eisma-Osorio joined Oceana Philippines as a consultant in 2015, a year after the NGO was established. At 56, she now leads the campaign and legal department as senior director of Oceana Philippines.

On October 24, 2025, a major ethanol wastewater spill hit Bais Bay, part of the Tañon Strait Protected Seascape (TSPS). Oceana Philippines collaborated with marine scientists to assess the severity of the spill. Their research, with the latest report in July this year, found that Universal Robina Corporation’s (URC) ethanol plant continued to leak wastewater, killing fish, corals and seagrass. The NGO is also consulting with fishing communities to build a court case against the company.

With more than 25 years of experience in natural resources law and policy, Eisma-Osorio believes it’s her personal responsibility to ensure there is legal accountability. In an interview with Mongabay via video call, she talked about representing marine mammals, the reaction from the community, and her current legal fight.

Mongabay: What was your thought process in deciding to represent the marine mammals in such a landmark case?

Rose Liza Eisma-Osorio: It was an ambitious undertaking. We wanted to challenge the thinking that only humans can file cases in court. And we knew there were two ways it could go: the court would throw out the case or decide to hear it. So we wanted to be sure, and we had Attorney Ramos and myself to act as stewards representing the marine mammals.

If you look at the case caption, the marine mammals were joined and represented by us, meaning they were also signing as individuals while being represented by us, because if the court did not allow them to join as litigants, it could still allow us to represent the dolphins and whales.

Mongabay: How was the case received back then, by communities, environmental groups, and even the court?

Eisma-Osorio: Around that time, what was refreshing about the campaign was that there was already an organic movement, especially the Save Tañon Strait Movement. There were very active Cebuanos, individuals, and students who helped raise awareness. The fisherfolk we represented were part of it too, so there was community engagement, because we knew they were the injured party in a way.

That was also the strategy behind two petitions. In the Philippines, you have to suffer an injury for the court to say you’re entitled to the remedy. We wanted the fisherfolk to prove their reduced catch and be heard, in the event that the court did not listen to the resident marine mammals case, since proof of injury was still a big question mark at that time.

Mongabay: At what point did you say, ‘This case is winnable?’ What was the turning point in lobbying to represent the resident marine mammals, especially with court updates?

Eisma-Osorio: We didn’t expect it to be in our favor. When we filed it in December 2007, the turning point was that even before the court decided, JAPEX pulled out. That was our early victory.

Then in 2015, the court decided in our favor, which was an added bonus. What the court zeroed in on, and what made it a landmark case, is that you don’t have to show proof of personal injury to represent nature as stewards and give nature legal standing in court. Only that you are here representing nature and this is the damage that was done.

We were surprised, and we said, “OK, we’ve set a precedent in Philippine jurisprudence.” This makes it easier for our citizens to file environmental cases now.

Mongabay: What immediate effect did you see after the Supreme Court decision?

Eisma-Osorio: After we won the case, I became Oceana’s consultant, and we decided to work on the management plan for Tañon Strait, because even if it was established as a protected seascape in 1998, there was no management plan at all.

Our contribution went beyond the case, [we got] into managing the area well and enforcing the laws and rules there. We left a living document that allows the agencies and local governments to work together to manage Tañon Strait in a better way.

Mongabay: Nine months after the October 2025 ethanol spill in Bais Bay, Silliman University marine scientists found the pollution killed up to 69 percent of coral cover in the assessed reef areas. What does it mean for Oceana to lobby again for the community?

Eisma-Osorio: Tañon Strait will always be our legacy campaign. When there are challenges like the ethanol spill, we need to go back and do our part.

We worked with the scientists from Silliman University to elevate the issue into a national concern, and we were pleasantly surprised by how our [press release] became viral. The communications tool is always useful, and it helped move the Department of Environment and Natural Resources. They have filed a criminal action against the responsible officers of URC, and I think the case is now ongoing.

But there’s still the matter of the ongoing leakage that continues to affect the fishing communities. And if it’s not stopped, then it might become worse and turn the bay into a wasteland.

We’re not entirely satisfied, because there are legal tools like the Writ of Kalikasan that could ensure the bay is restored and responsible actors are held accountable.

It’s early days, but there is an opportunity to ensure the community gets the justice it deserves for the damage to their resources and livelihood. Bais Bay is small compared to the entire stretch of Tañon Strait, but it’s ground zero for some because it’s where you do the dolphin and whale watching. If livelihoods are thriving there, you’ve protected Tañon Strait. That’s why it’s my personal quest to ensure environmental justice for what happened in Bais Bay.

Mongabay: Do you think it’s going to be a long battle ahead?

Eisma-Osorio: Yes, it will be a long battle ahead. We will be battling this together with the community. Nothing about them should be without them.
